papers.title: Chips & Tokens at the Fault Lines: Two Stacks in One Fragmenting World
papers.abstract: The United States and China have each built the capacity to inflict serious economic damage on each other. This paper argues that the resulting mutual vulnerability now constrains both sides and prevents further economic decoupling. The paper maps this contest across two stacks: the real economy stack of computing, semiconductors and rare earths, and the financial stack of dollar dominance and digital finance. On the real side, an analysis of global earnings call reports, run through large language models, suggests that this mutual vulnerability was already shaping the global corporate narrative in 2025. On the financial side, the paper argues that digital finance could tip this balance either way. Portable U.S. dollar-denominated digital assets could deepen U.S. dollar dominance and erode China's capital controls, tilting the balance toward Washington and inviting more fragmentation. A drift of transactions onto offshore rails like Tether could do the opposite, eroding Washington’s enforcement power behind sanctions and, counterintuitively, restraining it. Both the U.S. and China, meanwhile, run internally inconsistent policies. The U.S. is closing its door to trade while keeping an open financial account, and China is doing the reverse. These configurations are ultimately unsustainable and could undermine the arsenals that sustain the equilibrium.

papers.title: Valuing the Cost of Incomplete Global Markets
papers.abstract: Deviations from complete financial markets in cross-border investments generate economic welfare costs. This paper shows how to value these costs using standard theory and data based on three main results. Our first result shows how welfare valuations can be derived from a general wealth-to-dividend ratio. Next, we establish how aggregate consumption and exchange rate data can be used to uncover diversifiable goods allocations across countries. Finally, we demonstrate how asset pricing data and models can be used to value deviations from complete markets. The paper outlines a range of applications that fall under this framework, including financial intermediary constraint models.

papers.title: Long-run Uncovered Interest Parity in Emerging Markets
papers.abstract: Uncovered interest parity (UIP) tends to hold at long horizons for advanced-economy currencies. Whether it holds in emerging markets remains a more open question. We show it does not, and that sovereign credit risk can explain the failure. Using monthly zero-coupon local-currency yield curves for all emerging market currencies for which they are available from 2000 to 2025, we find that the slope of long-horizon UIP regressions is well below one at the five-year maturity for emerging market currencies, while unity cannot be rejected for G10 currencies. However, when we augment these regressions with sovereign CDS spreads, this slope rises to values statistically indistinguishable from one for floating emerging market currencies. The correction works best for currencies whose credit risk is most variable. A no-arbitrage asset pricing framework guides the specification of the regressions and the interpretation of the results.
